paper_summary: This paper presents GRADINO, a from-scratch generator and diagnostic benchmark framework for numerical question answering over multiple non-relational (pivoted, hierarchical, noisy) tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (schema + data), derives executable SQL programs to compute verifiable scalar answers, and renders perturbed non-relational views (pivots, merged headers, blank rows, OCR/noise, unit changes) from the same latent source. It verbalizes SQL programs into natural-language questions and uses a verification pass to filter/repair questions. The generator supports two multi-table evidence-flow topologies: parallel (extract one scalar per table then aggregate) and sequential (propagate lookup keys across table chain then aggregate). Experiments in financial and environmental domains evaluate contemporary LLMs (gpt-5-mini and Qwen family) and show sharp, compounded performance drops from non-relational presentation, table count scaling, and unit heterogeneity. The paper also shows GRADINO-generated data can complement scarce in-domain supervision and includes a manual verification of question fidelity and ablations on real perturbed tables.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Well-motivated: addresses an important, under-explored real-world problem—numerical multi-table reasoning over non-relational table presentations. 2) Methodological clarity: clean separation between latent SQL supervision and perturbed non-relational views preserves verifiability while enabling diverse, controlled perturbations. 3) Thorough experiments: scaling analyses (up to 20 tables for parallel), domain-aware unit heterogeneity studies, ablations, tests on perturbed real tables, and manual verification of generated questions. 4) Utility: shows generated data improves fine-tuned models on a scarce in-domain benchmark and provides code/prompts/appendices to aid reproducibility. 5) Practical diagnostic value: pinpoints specific failure modes (multi-table scaling, unit mismatch, sequential lookup difficulty) that are actionable for future work.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Limited realism of synthetic data: by design GRADINO is a controlled, synthetic generator and the authors acknowledge it may not capture all distributional and visual regularities of real spreadsheets and reports. This constrains direct generalization to all real-world documents. 2) LLM-based question verbalization dependence: questions are generated and verified by LLMs, which can omit or hallucinate constraints; although manual inspection shows high fidelity, verbalization errors remain a potential confound. 3) Model coverage in experiments: evaluation focuses on gpt-5-mini and Qwen-family models; results might differ for other strong systems or production tool chains (e.g., models using specialized table pre-processing). 4) Complexity of constraint choices: semi-automatic constraint enforcement using Z3 is powerful but adds complexity; the effects of different constraint sets on difficulty and realism could be explored further. 5) Limited analysis of downstream user impact: the paper documents LLM failures but does not quantify the real-world consequences of these errors in deployed analytic workflows (e.g., economic/regulatory implications).
comments_suggestions_typos: Minor suggestions: (a) explicitly state the planned release location and contents (code, datasets, seeds, prompt files) early in the main paper for reproducibility. (b) In the evaluation, adding at least one additional closed-model baseline (if allowed) or clarifying why it was not included would strengthen claims about generality. (c) Include a short worked example in the main text that traces a single sequential instance end-to-end (latent SQL → rendered views → NL question → model output) to aid readers. (d) Small formatting/figure clarifications in appendices (clarify some legend entries and table captions). No critical typos detected that affect understanding.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss limitations (synthetic realism, restricted numerical structure, question verbalization errors, discarded generations) and data/privacy considerations (synthetic data contains no PII; real tables used for validation come from public sources). They caution that GRADINO is a diagnostic complement rather than a replacement of real benchmarks. One further societal note: numerical errors in financial or environmental reports can have real consequences; the paper frames GRADINO as a tool to surface such failure modes, but a follow-up study quantifying practical impacts or mitigation strategies for downstream deployments would be valuable.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical concerns identified. The authors generate synthetic fictional data and use public datasets only for validation. They report licenses and treat data non-commercially. Use of LLMs and synthetic generation is documented; potential model bias or training-data contamination risks are acknowledged in related work but do not raise direct ACL Code of Ethics violations here.
